metaTitle: Pallet Glossary: Pallet Terms A to Z — AGL Pallet
metaDescription: Plain definitions of pallet terms from A to Z: deckboards, stringers, blocks, notches, entry types, GMA, HT, MB, ISPM-15, load ratings, racking, and more.
intro: Definitions are written for buyers and are kept short. Where a term has a full guide, the definition links to it. Industry usage varies, so confirm any term that matters to an order in the written spec.

terms.definition: ANSI MH1-2021, an ANSI-approved standard covering pallets, slip sheets, and other unit load bases, including terminology, dimensions, and test methods. The 2021 edition is the one the publisher lists.
The USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which enforces U.S. import rules for wood packaging material.
The American Lumber Standard Committee. It accredits the inspection agencies that license and monitor U.S. facilities treating wood packaging under ISPM-15.
ASTM International's standard test methods for pallets and related structures. The current reaffirmation on the publisher page is D1185-98a(2025).
The share of a truck's gross weight carried by one axle or axle group. A load can be under the gross limit and still over an axle limit if it is not spread along the trailer.
The list of every board in a pallet design with quantity, thickness, width, and length, plus fasteners. The clearest way to state a pallet spec.
Deckboards placed end to end to span a pallet when a single board is not long enough. Written specs often limit or prohibit them.
A solid or composite spacer, usually wood, that sits between the top and bottom decks of a block pallet in place of stringers. A 48 × 40 block pallet commonly uses nine blocks.
A pallet built on blocks rather than continuous stringers, giving true four-way entry for both forklifts and pallet jacks. Common in pooled and automated systems.
A lumber volume of 144 cubic inches, such as a board 1 inch thick, 12 inches wide, and 12 inches long. Lumber is often priced by the board foot.
The boards on the underside of a pallet. A bottom deck spreads the load on conveyors, racking, and stacked pallets.
The federal formula that limits the weight on groups of axles based on how far apart they are, so heavy loads do not overstress bridges.
The ability of a pallet to carry a load across an unsupported span, such as between rack beams. Poor bridging shows up as deflection or sagging.
A large piece of lumber sawn on two or more sides that is later resawn into deckboards or stringers.
A bevel cut along the edge of a bottom deckboard, usually at the pallet's entry ends, that helps pallet jack wheels roll onto and off the bottom deck.
A pallet pooling company whose blue pallets are rented to shippers and returned through its network rather than sold. See pooled pallet.
A second stringer fastened alongside a damaged one as a repair. Its presence is one of the marks that separates Grade B from Grade A in common usage.
One of the four blocks at the corners of a block pallet. Corner blocks take the most impact from forklifts and are a common repair point.
A pallet made from corrugated paperboard. Light and not wood, so outside ISPM 15, but low in strength and weak when wet.
A wooden enclosure, open or sheathed, built around a load on a base. Used for machinery and parts that need protection on all sides.
The usable interior volume of a trailer or container. A load "cubes out" when it fills the space before it reaches the weight limit.
Lumber that has been sawn to the finished lengths, widths, and thicknesses a pallet design calls for, ready for assembly.
Wood with its bark removed. ISPM 15 requires wood packaging to be made from debarked wood, within small stated tolerances.
The share of a deck's surface covered by boards rather than gaps. Higher coverage supports small cartons and bags better and adds weight and cost.
Any board that forms the top or bottom surface of a pallet. Deckboards run perpendicular to stringers on a stringer pallet.
The gaps between deckboards. Wide gaps save wood but can let small cartons or bag corners drop through or snag.
How far a pallet bends under load. Racked and free-span loads are usually limited by acceptable deflection, not just by breaking strength.
An ISPM-15 treatment that heats wood with microwave or radio-frequency energy. Marked DH on the treatment stamp.
A trailer with a second floor partway up, so pallets that cannot be stacked on each other can still use the trailer's height.
A pallet with both a top and a bottom deck. If the decks match, it is reversible.
A pallet whose top and bottom deckboards both extend past the outer stringers. Used for sling and crane handling.
A square pallet, such as 48 × 48 or 42 × 42, sized to carry drums.
An enclosed, unrefrigerated trailer. The 53 ft dry van is the standard North American truckload trailer.
Loose wood or other material used to brace, block, or separate cargo in transit. Wood dunnage crossing a border falls under ISPM-15.
The ISPM-15 mark code for dunnage. It is added to the treatment stamp when the wood is loose bracing or blocking rather than a pallet, crate, or box.
The load a pallet can carry while it is being moved by a forklift or pallet jack. Usually lower than the static rating.
A pallet designed to a stated load, support condition, and handling system rather than picked from a stock list.
The openings between decks where forklift tines or pallet jack forks go in. Pallets are described as two-way or four-way by how many sides allow entry.
The European Pallet Association, which licenses the production and repair of EPAL Euro pallets and runs an open exchange pool.
A 1200 × 800 mm block pallet common in Europe, managed under the EPAL exchange system when marked accordingly.
An open pallet pool in which trading partners swap pallets of an agreed type and quality instead of returning them to a single owner.
Another name for a one-way pallet: built to make one trip and not expected back.
The nails, staples, or screws that hold a pallet together. Fastener type, length, and pattern have a large effect on durability.
The moisture content, roughly 30% for many species, below which wood starts to shrink as it dries.
A pallet whose deckboards end flush with the outer stringers or blocks, with no overhang.
A pallet's length and width, stated with the stringer length first in North America, such as 48 × 40.
A pallet that allows entry from all four sides. See partial four-way and true four-way.
A pallet supported only at two edges, as on rack beams, with nothing under the middle. The most demanding way to support a loaded pallet.
A shipment that uses a whole trailer, priced for the truck rather than by the pallet. Usually the lowest freight cost per pallet.
Treating wood with a gas to kill pests. Methyl bromide (MB) is the fumigant recognized in ISPM 15.

The 48 × 40 inch (1219 × 1016 mm) stringer pallet footprint popularized by the Grocery Manufacturers Association for grocery and consumer-goods shipping. The association became the Consumer Brands Association in 2020; the pallet trade still uses the GMA name.
A trade label, such as A, B, #1, or #2, describing a pallet's condition or lumber quality. Grade names are not a published standard.
Lumber that has not been dried and still holds a high moisture content. Common in pallet building; it shrinks and lightens as it dries.
The total weight of a truck, trailer, and load. The federal limit on the Interstate system is 80,000 lb, subject to axle limits.
A pallet roughly half a standard footprint, such as 48 × 20 or 24 × 40 in North America, used for store displays and smaller loads.
Lumber from broadleaf trees such as oak or poplar. In pallets, hardwood is common in the eastern United States and tends to be dense and heavy.
An ISPM-15 treatment in which the wood core reaches at least 56 °C (133 °F) for 30 continuous minutes. Marked HT on the treatment stamp.
The International Plant Protection Convention, the international treaty body that adopts ISPM-15 and owns the wheat-ear symbol used in treatment marks.
The ISO standard listing principal dimensions for flat pallets used in intercontinental handling, including 1219 × 1016 mm (48 × 40 in).
International Standard for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15, which sets treatment and marking rules for wood packaging in international trade.
Lumber dried in a kiln to a target moisture content. Kiln drying controls moisture; it is not the same as heat treatment for ISPM-15.
The base of a branch embedded in a board. Large or loose knots weaken deckboards and stringers and are limited in most pallet specs.
The outermost deckboard at each end of the top deck, often wider or thicker because it takes forklift impact.
A shipment that shares a trailer with other freight and is priced by weight, class, and distance. Common for small pallet orders.
The weight a pallet can safely carry under stated support conditions: static, dynamic, or racked.
A fumigant approved under ISPM-15 but restricted in many countries because it depletes ozone. Marked MB on the treatment stamp.
A steel or aluminum pallet, used for very heavy loads, high heat, or closed loops. Not wood, so outside ISPM 15.
The weight of water in wood as a percentage of its oven-dry weight. It affects pallet weight, shrinkage, fastener holding, and mold risk.
A handheld tool that reads the moisture content of wood. Useful when weighing pallets or checking lumber for mold risk.
Fungal growth on wet wood. Pallets built from green lumber and shipped or held in warm, closed spaces are most at risk.
A pallet designed to make repeated trips and come back to the shipper, usually heavier than a one-way design.
A pallet, usually plastic or presswood, whose legs fit into the pallet below when empty, so stacks take less space.
A double-face pallet whose bottom deck differs from the top, so only the top carries the load. The most common stringer pallet style.
A cutout in the bottom of a stringer that lets forklift tines enter from the side, turning a two-way stringer pallet into a partial four-way pallet.
The government plant protection agency that enforces ISPM-15 in a country. In the United States it is USDA APHIS.
A pallet expected to make a single trip and not come back to the shipper. Often lighter and lower in cost than a multi-trip design.
Product or packaging that extends past the pallet's edge. Overhang weakens cartons and can cause damage in transit.
A hinged wooden frame that sits on a pallet and stacks with others to form a box around the load. Common in Europe.
A practice in which the receiver returns an equal number of empty pallets for the loaded ones just delivered, instead of the shipper buying or renting each pallet.
A hand or powered truck with forks that slide under a pallet and lift it just off the floor. Its wheels need open bottom-deck space to enter.
A plant that builds pallets from lumber. AGL is a brokerage: it places orders with qualified mills.
A system in which pallets are owned by a pool operator or shared under exchange rules, rather than owned by each shipper.
A notched stringer pallet: forklifts enter all four sides, but pallet jacks enter only the two unnotched ends.
The weight a truck can legally carry once the tractor and trailer weight is taken out of the gross limit.
A U.S. pallet pooling company whose red block pallets are rented to shippers and remain PECO's property.
A loading pattern that alternates pallet orientations around a center to fill a floor more fully than straight rows.
A molded pallet made from plastic resin. Exempt from ISPM-15 and often used in closed loops, food, and pharma.
A pallet rented from a pallet pool and returned through the pool's network rather than bought outright.
A Bureau of Labor Statistics index of the prices domestic producers receive. BLS publishes one for wood pallets.
A molded pallet made from wood fibers and resin under heat and pressure. Processed wood, so exempt from ISPM-15, and often nestable.
Wood material such as plywood, OSB, or presswood made with glue, heat, and pressure. Exempt from ISPM 15 treatment.
The load a pallet can carry while supported on rack beams. Usually the lowest of the three ratings.
Steel shelving systems that hold loaded pallets off the floor, usually on two beams. Racked pallets need a rating for the rack's support condition.
A pallet rebuilt from salvaged components. AGL sources new pallets only.
A double-face pallet whose top and bottom decks are identical, so either side can carry the load.
Lumber sawn to size but not planed smooth. Common in pallets; its dimensions vary more than planed lumber.
A heavy board or timber under a skid that raises the deck off the floor, doing the job stringers do on a pallet.
A pallet with a top deck only and no bottom deck.
A pallet whose top deckboards extend past the outer stringers while the bottom deck is flush.
A fumigant approved under ISPM-15. Marked SF on the treatment stamp. Confirm the destination country accepts it before specifying SF.
A platform with runners or stringers and no bottom deck. Often used for heavy machinery and loads that stay put.
A thin sheet of fiberboard or plastic that replaces a pallet under a unit load, moved with a push-pull forklift attachment.
Lumber from conifers such as Southern Yellow Pine or spruce. Lighter than most hardwoods and common in pooled and export pallets.
A deck with no gaps between boards, or a sheet deck, for small cartons, bags, or loads that must not snag.
Wood's density relative to water, based on oven-dry weight. Published by species; the basis for estimating pallet weight.
A crack through a board, often at the ends. Splits near fasteners reduce holding strength and are limited in pallet specs.
The load a pallet can carry sitting on a flat floor, not moving. Usually the highest of the three ratings.
Plastic film wrapped around a loaded pallet to hold the unit load together in transit.
A continuous board running the length of a pallet between the decks. A 48 × 40 stringer pallet usually has three.
A pallet built on stringers rather than blocks. The most common construction for one-way and domestic shipping in North America.
On a block pallet, the board that runs across the tops of the blocks and ties them together under the top deck.
The weight of packaging or equipment without the product, such as an empty pallet or an empty trailer.
A pallet nail with helical or ring threads on the shank that resists pulling out better than a smooth nail.
One of the forks on a forklift. Tine spacing and entry height decide which pallets a forklift can handle.
The load-carrying surface of a pallet. Top deckboard count and spacing set how well the deck supports cartons.
The bordered ISPM-15 mark showing the IPPC symbol, a country code and producer number joined by a hyphen, a treatment code, and DUN when the wood is dunnage.
A pallet, usually block construction, that both forklifts and pallet jacks can enter from all four sides.
Loading 48 × 40 pallets with the 40-inch side along the trailer, which fits 30 on the floor of a typical 53 ft van instead of 26.
A pallet that allows entry from only two opposite sides, such as an unnotched stringer pallet.
Product, packaging, and pallet handled together as one piece. Pallet design is best judged as part of the whole unit load.
Bark or missing wood along the edge of a board, left where the board was cut near the log's surface. Limited in most pallet specs.
A board that is no longer flat or straight, such as bow, cup, or twist, often from uneven drying.
A trade term for an unpainted wood pallet that is not part of a rental pool and is owned by whoever bought it.
The portion of a deckboard that extends beyond the outer stringer. See double-wing pallet.
Pallets, crates, dunnage, and other wood used to support or protect cargo. The category regulated by ISPM 15.
The U.S.-based wood packaging trade association that publishes the Uniform Standard for Wood Pallets, 2025 edition.
